title: Iti pi so
hookLine: a line under the breath before a night drive: protection, or a steadier mind?
tomorrow: the chant praises the Buddha, then his teaching. who comes third?

lines: A LINE BEFORE THE ENGINE STARTS.
cards: Some people tap the dashboard before a long drive. Some touch a medal on the mirror, or say a line under their breath as the engine starts. In some cars, that line is in Pali: iti pi so bhagava.
Thus indeed is he, the Blessed One. Ask two people in the same family why, and you can get two answers. Grandpa says it protects the car.
Mom says it just calms him down. They're both quoting the same old text.

teach.h: ITI PI SO: THUS INDEED IS HE.
teach.b: First, the words. Iti pi so bhagava: thus indeed is he, the Blessed One. Then the Buddha's qualities, one by one.
Araham: worthy. Sammasambuddho: fully awake, by himself. Sugato: well-gone.
Lokavidu: knower of the worlds. Sattha devamanussanam: teacher of gods and humans. Now, the text both sides quote.

In the Samyutta, the Buddha tells a story about the top of the banner. When the gods go to battle, their king says: if you're afraid, look up at my banner, and your fear will go. Then the Buddha turns it to his monks.
If fear comes on you in the forest, at the foot of a tree, in an empty hut, recollect me: iti pi so. And fear will go.

teach.h: ONE VIEW: A CHANT THAT PROTECTS.
teach.b: One view, heard in Theravada temples: this is a protection chant, one of the paritta. The Buddha's qualities are real and true, and chanting that truth guards the one who chants and the ones who hear.
At blessings, monks may chant it over water and thread. The other view, held too: the protection is the recollection.

teach.h: ANOTHER: A MIND TURNED TO THE GOOD.
teach.b: Calling those qualities to mind turns the mind away from panic and toward something steady and good, and that's what the sutta means.
Both sides hold the same verse. Both say it, before the drive.

how: Theravada monks chant the Dhajagga Sutta, with its verses on the qualities of the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha, as one of the protection chants at blessings; lay Buddhists recite iti pi so at home, before travel, or as a recollection in meditation.

o: a blessing asking the Buddha to keep travelers safe
the opening words that praise the Buddha's qualities
the name of the banner carried before an army

games.q: the Buddha's qualities — tap the pairs.
p: thus indeed is he, the Blessed One

s: chanting iti pi so for protection has no root in the old texts
in the Samyutta's banner story, the Buddha tells frightened monks to recollect him this way, and fear will go.
Buddhists who chant it agree on exactly how it helps
some hold it a protection chant whose truth guards the chanter; others hear the recollection itself as the protection.
the sutta compares recollecting the Buddha to looking up at a banner
the gods' king tells his frightened army to look at his banner's top; the Buddha gives his monks iti pi so.

games.q: your aunt keeps iti pi so on a card in her car and says the words themselves guard her. your cousin rolls her eyes. what's the aunt's best case?
o: the sutta itself says recalling the Buddha drives off fear, and the verse's truth is held to protect.
any words in Pali work like a lucky charm, whatever they happen to mean.
the card protects the car whether or not anyone ever reads it.
games.why: the protection view stands on the banner sutta and the paritta tradition: true words about the Buddha, chanted, guard the one who chants. the other view reads the same sutta as a mind turned to the good.

practice: Chant the opening line once, out loud or under your breath: iti pi so bhagava araham sammasambuddho. Then close your eyes and keep one quality for the sit, worthy or fully awake.
When a worry shows up, look up at the banner: come back to the line.

wordCard.voice: Iti pi so: thus indeed is he. The opening of the verse on the Buddha's qualities, chanted for courage and for calm.

orig.note: Pali, in Devanagari letters: iti pi, thus indeed; so, he; bhagava, the Blessed One.

carryVoice: For the road: thus indeed is he, said slowly, in the dark or in daylight. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: SN 11.3 (Dhajagga Sutta, 'the top of the banner'): the gods' king's banner; the Buddha tells monks afraid in the forest to recollect him, iti pi so bhagava …, and fear will go
The recollection of the Buddha (iti pi so bhagava araham sammasambuddho … sattha devamanussanam buddho bhagava)
